title: What game engine to use?
author: Mission_Engineer_999
selftext:
Hi guys, I am curious about AI game development and have a couple of questions.

1. Is there an engine that lends itself to work with ai better than others, be it unity or godot or whatever else?

2. Github Copilot vs ChatGPT desktop app. Any appreciable difference?

3. I cannot draw to save my life. What would be the best approach for me to outsource this to AI, i.e. get premade assets to use as derivatives or have AI do it all from scratch?

Say, if it were a 2d sprite game.

Any input would be welcome.

comments.author: 3tt07kjt
comments.body: Your advice is completely backwards. I see this approach a lot, and most people who follow it end up not shipping games-they end up diving into irrelevant engine development tasks in order to avoid dealing with the challenges of game design.

replies.author: Aggravating-Vehicle9
replies.body:
I think you probably should use an engine if your goal is to make a commercially viable game. In general, I guess my scepticism is whether one can expect one's first game to be a commercially viable product.

There's so much to learn about game development that simply adopting an engine denies the opportunity to learn certain things that you probably need to know before you're able to appreciate just what that engine is doing for you and the decisions and values that were baked into that engine and the justifications that have been developed over decades of video game development history.

Clearly, if there's an engine out there that's going to help you, it's going to get you closer to releasing something viable. You can lean on the development of others, but when you're just beginning your journey, when you're learning, I feel that using an engine can hinder some of the fundamental learning that you really do need in order to know what you're doing.

replies.author: 3tt07kjt
replies.body:
I think you should use an engine if you are interested in making a game on your own to learn or for fun. 

There’s so much to learn about game development that the only way you can hope to make progress is to pick and choose what you are interested in, and then specialize. 

Picking an engine lets you start in a pretty good place—making a game, making things move around on screen, and you’re not deep in the weeds, technically. This is the best starting point. You can go and make your own engine if you are more interested in that. Or you can go in the opposite direction, and decide that you want to focus on art, narrative, or gameplay. 

Starting with just code will definitely hinder your journey if you don’t already know that you are specifically interested in that kind of work. I’ve seen it.

comments.author: Crazy_Amphibian_8440
comments.body: chatgpt and claude are neck and neck in benchmarks but chatgpt can generate images and videos to be used as assets in the game aswell. the anthropic shilling needs to stop. generating assets is objectively a major advantage in gamedev.

replies.author: Crazy_Amphibian_8440
replies.body:
\> they’re comparable at coding tasks  
\>gamedev sub (hence asset generation)

comments.author: vlaaad
comments.body: Given that llms can work with any game engines, you should choose an engine based on the features that are important for your project. For example, for desktop-only games, probably any free engine will be good. For web-only, you might need smallest builds, so maybe just a js lib. If you want multiplatform that works both on mobile, desktop, and in the browser, Defold is a good choice

comments.author: Necessary_Weight
comments.body:
Godot. If your choice is between Github Copilot and Codex/ChatGPT, Codex with Astra on High any time. GPT can do awesome 2d art. Claude does better but if you want one sub with image capability, I would personally recommend $200 Open AI sub.

One caveat. For UI work, I prefer to prototype it in Typescript and then port it to Godot. Results for me are amazing

comments.author: SerenityScott
comments.body: I'm not clear on what an engine gives me. I'm making games with the claude app that run on [itch.io](http://itch.io) . Claudes seems to have a good understanding already of game implementation best practices (like how the controller should feel as far as stick and movement response). I don't have to tune any of that.

replies.author: 3tt07kjt
replies.body:
You’re missing out on a massive set of dev tools and foundation work. Things like level editors and ways to tweak values live or edit objects in the engine by pointing and clicking. 

You can prompt Claude to make those changes like “make the character 10% taller” but this is a kind of slow and tedious way of doing it. 

I’ve had Claude build these tools out for me but it’s taken days or weeks to get things built that would have been available from day zero had I used an engine. 

I’ve used an engine before so I know what I’m missing, and I’m missing a lot.

replies.author: SerenityScott
replies.body: ok cool. I'm new to this and have never used a game engine before, so I'm learning. in modern stuff I've only written text games with python, and before that it was... super pascal on a 386, then applesoft basic before that?  Oh I guess I tried Ansi C once to do a sprite rpg in linux in the 90s but never got far with that... was having to build everything myself and ran out of time.

replies.author: 3tt07kjt
replies.body:
Yeah. I had a similar starting point. You can keep making games that way, you can try out an engine, and you can have AI just code everything from the ground up.

I’ve been making games both ways (with and without engines) and it’s amazing how much useful stuff engines do for you. So that’s where I recommend to start.

replies.author: BinniesPurp
replies.body:
It's like Microsoft excel for video games 

It comes prepacked with maths, AI, physics etc and also provides a workplace / interface for you to directly edit within

comments.author: fukinuhhh
comments.body:
Unreal will probably become the best because they are innovating the most with AI integration. They showcased the new tools recently with unreal 5.9 

However, 5.9 isn't complete, you can download it but expect bugs. I've used unreal 5.8 with Claude, and it works pretty good. For a 2-D game it's probably overkill though.

comments.author: ZyronZA
comments.body:
The difference between Codex Sol 6.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 is not nearly as wide as people make it out to be, but there is a difference and it currently favours Claude.

Chase value for money. Not brand loyalty.

comments.author: dantemp
comments.body:
You should ask your ai which engine it likes the most. I use Claude and it works incredibly well in Godot. However Godot itself is a bit limiting, like it cant even run dlss without some magic. But for a 2d game it's probably good enough. 

For assets ai assets are always lacking, but you can probably ask the ai itself, describe exactly what you want to do and ask it to give you a few options and explain the differences. There's some things you can do to get not awful results, but it's long way away from matching a good artist.

comments.author: Capybarhigh
comments.body:
That Unity take is so baffling with absolutely no argument to back it up that it completely dismisses the rest of your message as believable.

Unity works amazingly for me. Claude can run it headless, create scenes, take screenshots, work with assets. It works by itself, judging its own work in no time, to improve upon my requests. There are so many assets available on the store, I cut short my work time by a lot. It's extremely well documented, more than anything else probably after all these years as the go to engine, that Claude has no issue solving problems. 

And Unity 7 is coming soon with tons of improvement for both graphics AND working with AI.

comments.author: GasimGasimzada
comments.body:
I tried godot recently and you can run your game without opening the editor. The models can generate / update scene via cli.

Frontier models also have good knowledge on the engine; so, you can just start without any skills or mcp.

Can't say much about others but apparently UE5.9 is going all in on AI; so will be interesting to see how thay works.
